prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "JPMORGAN CHASE & CO" (ticker JPM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "JPM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.

mission.statement: We aim to be the most respected financial services firm in the world, serving corporations and individuals.
mission.source: JPMorganChase "How We Do Business" principles document (company website), which also states its purpose: "Make Dreams Possible For everyone, everywhere, every day."
mission.plain: JPMorgan wants to be the most trusted and admired bank in the world for both companies and ordinary people.

about.plain: JPMorgan Chase is the biggest bank in the United States. Through Chase it keeps people's money safe in checking and savings accounts, gives out credit cards, car loans and home loans, and runs over 5,000 branches. It also helps big companies and governments raise money, buy and sell shares and bonds, and move money around the world. And it looks after investments for wealthy families and pension funds.
about.customers: About 94 million US consumers and small businesses, plus most of the Fortune 500, governments and big investors around the world.
about.everyday: The Chase bank branch, ATM or Sapphire credit card in many Americans' wallets is JPMorgan.

money.plain: (share of Q3 2026 managed revenue) advising companies, raising money, trading, lending to businesses, payments and custody
bank accounts, credit cards, home and car loans for people and small firms
managing money for wealthy families and institutions
an app-only bank account for UK savers, launched in 2021
tokenised deposits and blockchain payment rails for big companies

result.summary: JPMorgan has a wide moat: its $5.1 trillion balance sheet, low-cost deposit base, fortress capital and #1 positions in US deposits, card spending, investment-banking fees and markets revenue create scale and switching-cost advantages that let it earn about 20% returns on tangible equity, well above peers. Regulation and the sheer cost of matching its roughly $20B annual technology budget make the lead hard to erode.

pricingPower.evidence: It pays below-market rates on a huge base of sticky checking deposits and charges premium annual fees (Sapphire Reserve's fee was raised to $795 in 2025) while still adding 10.4 million new card accounts in 2025, but lending and trading prices are set by competitive markets.

moats.evidence: Chase and J.P. Morgan are among the most trusted financial brands; after crises in 2008 and 2023 depositors fled to JPMorgan as a safe haven.
Moving direct deposits, bill payments, cards, mortgages or a corporation's treasury and payment systems is painful, so checking and treasury relationships are very sticky.
Its payments, custody and trading franchises benefit from scale: more clients mean more flow and liquidity, making its markets and treasury services more valuable to the next client.

With $182.4B of 2025 revenue and $2.8 trillion of deposits it spreads compliance and roughly $20B of technology spend over the biggest base, and holds 11.1% of US retail deposits (2025, up from 8.1% in 2015).
Global investment banking, markets and custody are dominated by a handful of firms with enough capital and global reach, leaving room for few new entrants.
JPMorgan is the incumbent; fintechs and private-credit funds counter-position against banks rather than the other way round.
Its disciplined risk management ('fortress balance sheet') has let it come through the 2008 crisis and 2023 regional-bank turmoil stronger, buying Bear Stearns, WaMu and First Republic.
A deep management bench under Jamie Dimon and a national branch network reaching 69% of the US population are hard for rivals to replicate.

customers.evidence: JPMorgan serves 94 million customers, added 1.7 million net new checking accounts in 2025, reports a Net Promoter Score of about 66, and enjoys 22 straight years of positive asset-management client flows.

talent.evidence: With 319,000 employees it is a top destination for finance graduates and pays at the top of the industry; it awarded $20M-$30M retention stock grants in 2026 to keep its senior succession candidates.

product.evidence: It ranks #1 in global investment banking fees (Dealogic), #1 in markets revenue (Coalition Greenwich), #1 in treasury services and US credit card sales, and its J.P. Morgan Private Bank has been named the world's best by Global Finance.

threats: CEO succession: Jamie Dimon (in charge since 2005) is expected to hand over within a few years, with co-presidents Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh the leading candidates
A US recession or credit-card and commercial real estate losses (2025 credit provisions already rose to $14.2B)
Falling interest rates compressing net interest income, its largest revenue source
Stablecoins, tokenised deposits and fintechs pulling deposits and payments away from banks
Private-credit funds such as Apollo and Blackstone taking corporate lending share
Tougher capital rules or political pressure, such as caps on credit card interest rates
Cyber attacks or operational failures at the world's most systemically important bank

ceo.name: Jamie Dimon
ceo.background: Tufts University BA (psychology and economics), Harvard MBA; protege of Sandy Weill at American Express, Commercial Credit and Citigroup; CEO of Bank One (2000-2004) before it merged into JPMorgan

c1.evidence: JPMorgan is the clear leader of global banking (#1 in US deposits, IB fees and markets revenue), but banking is a mature industry rather than an emerging, fast-growing one.

c2.evidence: Clients choose it for safety, breadth (from checking accounts to global payments and capital raising in one firm) and execution, advantages built over decades of scale and capital that are very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Chase is a household name across the US and JPMorgan is widely seen as the default leader of Wall Street, with an NPS of about 66.

c4.evidence: Its purpose to 'make dreams possible for everyone, everywhere, every day' and initiatives like the $1.5 trillion security-and-resiliency financing plan show purpose, but the firm is run primarily for strong financial returns.

c6.evidence: “big, powerful, safe, Wall Street” - the impression is mostly positive about strength and reliability, tempered by general distrust of big banks and past fines.

c7.evidence: Global financial services is an enormous and steadily growing market tied to GDP and wealth creation, but it does not ride a fast secular trend like AI or EVs.

c8.evidence: It is expanding branches into new US states, digital banking in the UK (Chase UK), and blockchain payments (Kinexys), but size and regulation limit acquisitions of other big US banks.

m1.evidence: Dimon has a clear long-term view, expressed in his annual shareholder letters, on fortress balance sheets, technology investment (about $19.8B in 2026) and the role of banks in society.

m2.evidence: Though not the founder, Dimon has run JPMorgan for over 20 years like an owner, staying through a 2014 cancer diagnosis and 2020 heart surgery.

m4.evidence: Dimon stresses serving clients and communities and raised minimum wages for branch staff, but he is known as a demanding, top-down leader who pushed staff back to the office five days a week in 2025.

m5.evidence: He has built a strong 'fortress' culture of discipline and heavy technology and AI investment, but JPMorgan is not known for inventing breakthrough products.

m6.evidence: Dimon is deeply hands-on in the details of every business but has a finance and psychology background, not an engineering one.

m7.evidence: Dimon speaks out on public policy, education and economic opportunity and the firm funds community programmes such as its Detroit investment, but the bank has also paid large regulatory fines.

m7b.evidence: No verified record found here of Dimon giving a commencement address at Stanford, Harvard or MIT.

m8b.evidence: Dimon is famously blunt and outspoken, the best-known banker of his generation, regularly making headlines with comments on the economy, regulation and politics.

m9.evidence: Under Dimon, JPMorgan navigated 2008 and 2023 profitably, bought Bear Stearns, WaMu and First Republic, and grew net income from $29.1B in 2020 to $57.0B in 2025.

m10.evidence: JPMorgan is disciplined on costs and risk, but its $95.6B of 2025 expenses, top-tier pay and lavish new 270 Park Avenue headquarters do not make it a byword for frugality.

c10.evidence: It provides banking and credit to 94 million US customers and finances companies and governments worldwide, an important but largely invisible service rather than a life-changing product.

p2.evidence: Running a safe $5.1 trillion global bank is very hard and systemically important, but the products themselves (loans, deposits, trading) are widely offered.

f1.evidence: Total net revenue rose every year from $119.95B in 2020 to $121.6B, $128.7B, $158.1B, $177.6B and $182.4B in 2025, and was $157.4B in the first nine months of 2026.

f2.evidence: Gross margin does not apply to a bank, but pre-tax margin rose from 29.9% in 2020 to 39.8% in 2025.

f3.evidence: As a bank it carries $531.5B of borrowings and long-term debt (Sept 2026), but this is backed by $326.3B of cash and deposits with banks, a 13.9% CET1 ratio and $372.4B of positive shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Pre-tax income rose from $35.8B in 2020 to $72.6B in 2025 though it dipped in 2022 and 2025, and bank operating cash flow is volatile because it swings with trading balances.

v1.evidence: For many people the practical reason is safety and convenience, the biggest US branch and ATM network plus a top-rated app and card rewards, but rival banks offer similar basic products.

v2.evidence: JPMorgan is one of the most sought-after employers in finance and regularly appears on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies list, but long hours and a strict return-to-office policy draw criticism.

c5.evidence: If JPMorgan vanished overnight, tens of millions of Chase customers would lose access to their money and much of the world's dollar payments, trading and corporate financing would seize up.
